paras: The killing of a smallpox patient near Red Clay, Georgia, took place in mid-July 1882, when railroad laborers shot an unnamed Black man who had been quarantined in an isolated cabin and then set the cabin on fire. Warrants were issued against several men, but the local paper reported no conclusive evidence of who took part. A one-line wire item carried the killing across the country, and a fuller Georgia account was later reprinted as 'Murder as a Cure for Small-Pox.'

According to the Dalton Citizen, the man, 'whose name we failed to learn', appeared with smallpox in 'the upper end of this county' near Red Clay. Local citizens quarantined him in a cabin away from other houses and warned him to stay there until the disease had passed; by then he was convalescent. Nearby, workers were building the Red Clay & Ooltewah railroad connection, and the Dalton paper said that 'the negroes at work' on that line learned of the case.

Fearing that the disease would spread, several of the workers armed themselves one night and went to the cabin. They shot the man through the window as he lay in bed, set fire to the house and 'literally cremated the poor victim', then escaped. The wire versions said he was 'shot dead' by 'railroad hands' and burned in his cabin, or in 'the building in which he was stationed'.

The Dalton Citizen reported that warrants had been issued against several men but that there was 'no conclusive evidence' of who had taken part. No report of an arrest, inquest or trial appears in the coverage.

The wire item first appeared in national news digests between July 19 and 21, 1882, in Dakota, New Hampshire, Minnesota, Missouri and Connecticut papers, as a single sentence among other crimes and accidents. These digests named only 'railroad hands' as the attackers, and one Missouri paper misprinted the place as 'Red City'.

In Georgia, the Marietta Journal reprinted the Dalton Citizen's account on July 20 under the headline 'BRUTAL ACT OF NEGRO FIENDS', calling the killing 'unparalleled for brutality and fiendishness' and the attackers 'wretches'. Through August, papers in Wisconsin and elsewhere ran the same account, without the sentence on warrants and credited to a 'Georgia Citizen', under the title 'Murder as a Cure for Small-Pox'.
The date is uncertain: one wire version gives the 12th and another the 13th, while the Dalton paper said only 'a few nights ago'.

bases: A convalescent smallpox patient was shot and his quarantine cabin burned by railroad laborers who feared the disease would spread; the local account names the attackers as Black workers and gives no racial or criminal pretext (A2, A3).

Several armed men killed the man without any lawful authority (A2), but the papers give fear of the spread of smallpox as the only motive, not an accusation, punishment or racial offense, so the pretext element of the definition is not met (A2, A9).
A Red Clay wire dispatch (A3, A4) and the local Dalton Citizen account (A2) differ in wording and detail but agree that a man with smallpox was shot by railroad workers and burned in his building.
